subject: Post-demo: Dedicated assurances vs cloud bursting — follow-ups & tests
messages:
From: Aisha Rahman <aisha.rahman@redwood.ai>
To: Sarah Kim <sarah.kim@brighthealth.ai>, Tom Lee <tom.lee@brighthealth.ai>
Cc: Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>
Date: Sun, 9 May 2027 14:02:00 -0700
Subject: Post-demo recap + clarifying reserved capacity vs cloud-bursting asks

Hi Sarah / Tom —

Thanks again for taking the demo today. Quick recap and the follow-ups we promised: we want to make sure the evaluation you run exercises the exact scenarios that are gating your decision between a Dedicated reserved pool and a hyperscaler-bursting model.

Key items we discussed:
- Latency SLO: your target is p99 <= 180ms at 50 RPS for the 512-token clinical-summary workload.
- Availability: during peak hours (M–F 8am–6pm PST) you need 99.95% availability; you also asked about automatic fallback to lower-cost model variants when Dedicated capacity is saturated.
- Data controls: VPC + customer-managed KMS required for PHI.
- Cost visibility: token-level breakdowns and a per-route cost estimate for 100M tokens/month.

Deliverables we committed to:
1) A short test plan for Dedicated vs Hyperscaler-bursting that targets the p99/throughput points above (we'll include exact request mix).
2) Baseline micro-benchmarks (attached) from our staging cluster: representative latency numbers for your model family (gpt-med-small / 512 seq).
3) Clarify contract-level commitments for Dedicated (uptime SLA, reserved capacity definition, preemption/fallback policy) and the tradeoffs for a hybrid with burst to cloud.

Next steps / asks for BrightHealth:
- Can you confirm target QPS profile (avg vs peak) and % of requests that are >256 tokens?
- Share a sanitized prompt sample (or subset) we can use for end-to-end A/B quality checks.

I've attached the quick benchmark CSV we ran against a representative 8xA100 pool and a short draft MSA with the standard Dedicated schedule redlines (we call out termination and capacity clauses).

Proposed timeline:
- Mon (5/10): Redwood runs the Dedicated test harness against your sample payloads (we'll run both reserved-only and reserved+burst to hyperscaler).
- Wed (5/12): send consolidated results + a canary rollout plan and recommended contract language.

If that looks right, we'll proceed. Happy to hop on another 30-min call this week for any clarifications.

Thanks,
Aisha Rahman
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference
[Attachment: benchmark_results_v1.csv] [Attachment: redlines_MSA_BrightHealth.pdf]

From: Sarah Kim <sarah.kim@brighthealth.ai>

Cc: Tom Lee <tom.lee@brighthealth.ai>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>
Date: Mon, 10 May 2027 09:03:12 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-demo recap + clarifying reserved capacity vs cloud-bursting asks

Thanks Aisha — this is exactly what we needed. A few clarifications and questions from our side: 

1) Traffic profile: typical steady state is ~20 RPS, but we see daily peaks of ~55–60 RPS for ~20–30 minutes (6–8am PST and 5–6pm PST). Spiky behavior is our primary concern.
2) Token distribution: ~30% of requests exceed 256 tokens; ~8% are >1024.
3) Data sample: I'll upload a sanitized 200-request sample to the drive link you shared by EOD.

Questions:
- For Dedicated: do you guarantee reserved GPU availability for bursts (i.e., can we expect immediate scaling above base commit) or is bursting an asynchronous provisioning process?
- If we choose a hybrid (Dedicated + hyperscaler burst), will Redwood route traffic automatically to the burst path when Dedicated queueing is detected, and how quickly?
- For SLAs: can you share the exact wording you propose for availability and latency SLOs — we need something we can take to procurement.

Also, procurement asked whether there is a standard credit or service-level credit if a failover to hyperscaler leads to higher latency for queued requests.

Appreciate the attachments — we'll review the benchmarks and redlines and come back with consolidated feedback.

—Sarah
CTO, BrightHealth AI

From: Aisha Rahman <aisha.rahman@redwood.ai>
To: Sarah Kim <sarah.kim@brighthealth.ai>, Tom Lee <tom.lee@brighthealth.ai>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 11 May 2027 07:28:00 -0700
Subject: Re: Post-demo recap + clarifying reserved capacity vs cloud-bursting asks

Hi Sarah — thanks for the quick details and for uploading the sample. Answers inline below and proposed next steps: 

- Reserved GPU availability: Dedicated reserved capacity is always allocated to your account (not preemptible). Autoscaling above commit depends on policy: we offer two burst modes — instant burst (pre-warmed standby nodes billed at lower rate) and elastic burst (provision-on-demand to hyperscaler). Instant burst requires a short warm-up reservation and a slightly higher commit but provides fast failover. Elastic burst leverages hyperscaler and is typically provisioned within 60–90s under normal conditions.

- Automated routing: yes — our Smart Routing policy can be configured to detect queueing (queue depth threshold or p99 latency breach) and automatically route to the burst path you select (instant vs elastic). We include a per-route circuit-breaker to avoid cascading failures.

- SLA wording: for Dedicated we typically offer 99.95% availability on the control plane and 99.9% on the serving plane for reserved pools with a throughput guarantee based on the committed GPU count. For latency we publish guidance and per-route p99 guardrails; we can add a service credit clause for missed availability targets. I'll attach a redline that adds a 5% service credit tier for sustained incidents >4 hours.

- Service credit on failover: we don't provide credits specifically for transient higher latency during a configured failover if the routing policy is working as intended (designed behavior). For unplanned failovers due to capacity loss we can discuss credit language.

Proposed concrete test matrix we will run Mon–Tue (internal):
1) Baseline Dedicated-only at 50 RPS, 512 token mix (measure p50/p95/p99 latencies, error rate).
2) Dedicated + instant-burst (pre-warmed standby) — simulate a sustained 65 RPS spike for 30 minutes.
3) Dedicated + elastic-burst (hyperscaler) — simulate sudden spike to 100 RPS and measure failover time and p99 tail.

We'll share a short CSV summary and a replayable artifact (JMeter script) you can run in your environment.

Next steps:
- Marissa will coordinate the test harness and share the JMeter script.
- Rishi will run the Dedicated vs hyperscaler passes and send consolidated numbers by Wed (5/12).
- Aisha will follow up with suggested contract clause language for the SLA/credits.

If that matches your needs, we'll run the tests and regroup after results are in. Would you like a quick 20-min sync Wed morning to go over the findings?

Thanks,
Aisha
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference
[Attachment: benchmark_results_v1.csv]

From: Aisha Rahman <aisha.rahman@redwood.ai>
To: Marissa Cole <marissa.cole@redwood.ai>, Rishi Malhotra <rishi.malhotra@redwood.ai>
Date: Wed, 11 May 2027 09:15:00 -0700
Subject: INTERNAL: Follow-up actions for BrightHealth evaluation — test assignments + contract notes

Marissa / Rishi — internal summary and immediate asks (BrightHealth is very sensitive to p99 tail and wants deterministic burst behavior):

1) Test assignments:
- Rishi: run Dedicated-only baseline and elastic-burst (hyperscaler) pass. Target metrics: p50/p95/p99, error %, tail latency breakdown (queue time vs serve time). Use the attached CSV as request mix. Produce a replayable JMeter artifact.
- Marissa: assemble instant-burst pre-warm config and run the 65 RPS 30-minute spike test. Capture failover time and any warm-up jitter.

2) Contract / Procurement asks:
- We should propose two options in the MSA: (A) Dedicated with instant-burst (pre-warmed standby) and (B) Dedicated + elastic-burst (pay-as-you-go hyperscaler). Drafts should include explicit definitions for "reserved capacity", "pre-warmed standby", and "burst provisioning time".
- Add a service credit schedule: 5% credit for serving-plane availability <99.9% over a 30-day period; escalate to 10% for control-plane incidents >4 hours. Note: exclude configured and tested failovers (documented routing policies).

3) Quick wins for the call with Sarah: prepare a one-slide summary showing expected p99 improvement using instant-burst vs elastic-burst under their traffic profile.

Attachments referenced: benchmark_results_v1.csv, redlines_MSA_BrightHealth.pdf (see Drive link).

I'll own the SLA redlines. Rishi / Marissa — can you confirm you have bandwidth to run these tests today/tomorrow? We want results to send to BrightHealth Wed morning.

Thanks,
Aisha
Enterprise Sales, Redwood Inference
